subtype: Approach: panic selling at the bottom [Pitfall]
passage:
The prices fell for eleven days in a row. In his small town, Francis checked the phone at the tea stall, at the bus stop, and at night under the blanket. Videos on the phone said everything would go to zero.
On the twelfth day, hands shaking, Francis sold every unit and felt the knot in the stomach loosen at once. "At least it stops," Francis told Saurabh, the shopkeeper next door, who had said "wait" a week earlier.
Three months later, prices were back up. Saurabh, who had kept his holdings and added nothing new, said only, "It came back." The paper loss Francis had feared was now a real one, and the calm from selling was gone.
Francis stared at the number for a long time.

qa.q: How many days in a row did the prices fall?
qa.a: The prices fell for eleven days in a row.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when selling every unit?
qa.a: Francis was frightened and desperate to end the pain, and felt brief relief once the selling was done.

qa.q: What could Francis do differently if prices fall again?
qa.a: Francis could decide beforehand what would count as a reason to sell and check the news only on a fixed day.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt telling Francis "It came back"?
qa.a: Saurabh was probably sympathetic and did not want to gloat, given the plain, quiet remark.

grounding: The passage shows an investor who sells everything to stop the pain of daily losses, then watches prices recover without them so the loss becomes real.

subtype: Approach: panic selling at the bottom [Pitfall]
passage:
Every evening on the train home in Osaka, Kaito opened his investment app and watched the number fall. Minus eight percent. Minus fourteen. Online, people posted charts titled "It's only the beginning". He stopped sleeping well. His friend Valentina, who had lived through an earlier crash in Madrid, told him, "Don't decide anything this week."
On the worst Thursday, down twenty-six percent, he sold everything. The relief was instant. The red numbers were gone.
Over the next eight months the market climbed slowly back. By the following spring it was higher than before the fall. Kaito's money was still sitting in cash. He had turned a temporary drop into a real loss of a quarter of his savings.
He deleted the app, then reinstalled it, then couldn't bring himself to buy back in. "I sold at the exact bottom," he told Valentina. She didn't say "I told you so". She didn't need to.

qa.q: How far down was Kaito when he sold?
How did Kaito feel right after selling?
qa.a: Kaito felt instant relief that the red numbers were gone.

qa.q: What could Kaito have done instead of selling that Thursday?
qa.a: Followed Valentina's advice not to decide that week, thought about when he needed the money, and spoken to a qualified adviser.

qa.q: How might Valentina feel when Kaito admits he sold at the bottom?
qa.a: Valentina probably feels sad for him and chooses kindness over "I told you so".

grounding: It shows a young investor, fed by daily losses and online fear, selling everything to stop the pain and missing the recovery, so the loss becomes permanent.

subtype: Approach: panic selling at the bottom [Pitfall]
passage:
In the software office canteen, Pallavi scrolled through her phone at lunch every day that March. The colleagues' group chat was full of screenshots: minus eighteen percent, minus twenty-two. Someone forwarded a video saying the market would never recover. Pooja, from the next team, said quietly, "Didn't you say this money was for twenty years from now?"
Pallavi didn't answer. That night she sold all her funds.
The next morning in the canteen she felt lighter. "At least I've stopped the bleeding," she told Pooja.
By October the index had recovered most of the fall. By the next March it was above where it had been. Pallavi's money was still in her savings account, earning almost nothing, and the twenty-two percent she had lost was now permanent. Every time the canteen TV showed market news, she moved to another table.

qa.a: "Didn't you say this money was for twenty years from now?"

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel the morning after selling?
qa.a: Pallavi felt lighter and relieved, believing she had stopped the bleeding.

qa.q: What would have helped Pallavi before she sold?
qa.a: Taking Pooja's question seriously, stepping away from the fearful group chat, and speaking to a qualified adviser before acting.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Pallavi moving tables?
qa.a: Pooja may feel sympathy, sensing that Pallavi now feels regret or embarrassment whenever market news comes on.

grounding: It shows a young investor, swept up in colleagues' fear and falling numbers, selling everything and missing the recovery, so the loss becomes permanent.
